# Stateful Operators and State Management {#sec-stateful-operators}

::: {.callout-note title="Status: complete first draft"}
:::

Stateless operators have it easy. A `Selection`, a `Map`, a
`Projection` — each takes a record, transforms it, forwards it.
Nothing remembered, nothing to clean up, nothing that can grow
unbounded.

Stateful operators are where streaming gets interesting. A hash
join build accumulates one side of the join. A windowed aggregation
accumulates partial sums per group per window. A session window
operator accumulates per-session bookkeeping until the session
times out. State is the engine's memory of what has happened, and
it has to be kept correct, kept bounded, and kept usable across
worker threads.

This chapter walks through how NebulaStream manages stateful
operator state. The data structures are the runtime ones we met in
Chapter 12 (`HashMap`, `PagedVector`); the lifecycle is intricate
enough to warrant its own chapter.

---

## 16.1 The state architecture: handlers, hash maps, and PagedVectors {#sec-state-arch}

Every stateful operator in NebulaStream owns its state through an
*operator handler*. The handler is a runtime object — distinct from
the operator class itself — that holds the per-query state and
exposes it to both the build and probe halves of the operator pair.

Handlers are registered at query-startup time, identified by an
`OperatorHandlerId`, and torn down when the pipeline that owns them
is destroyed. The `OperatorHandlerId` is the join's "shared key" —
the build operator references it to know where to insert; the
probe operator references the same one to know where to look up.

The state itself almost always combines two structures:

- **A `HashMap`** keyed on the join key (or the grouping key). The
  hash map holds entries, each a fixed-size header plus a pointer
  to a value chain.
- **A `PagedVector`** of values for chained collisions or
  unbounded per-key history.

Both come from `nes-nautilus/`; both are designed for the JIT to
inline.

---

## 16.2 The hash join's state {#sec-hash-join-state}

For a hash join, the build operator inserts each input tuple into
the hash map keyed on the join key. Hash collisions chain at the
bucket head. The probe operator looks up incoming tuples by hash
and walks the chain emitting matches.

The interface is small:

```cpp
// nes-nautilus/include/Nautilus/Interface/HashMap/HashMap.hpp
class HashMap {
public:
    virtual ~HashMap() = default;
    virtual AbstractHashMapEntry* insertEntry(
        HashFunction::HashValue::raw_type hash,
        AbstractBufferProvider* bufferProvider) = 0;
    [[nodiscard]] virtual uint64_t getNumberOfTuples() const = 0;
};
```

The concrete implementation is `ChainedHashMap`, in
`nes-nautilus/src/Nautilus/Interface/HashMap/ChainedHashMap/ChainedHashMap.cpp`.
The insertion path is worth reading in full because it shows how
the hash map's storage is actually paged across `TupleBuffer`s:

```cpp
// nes-nautilus/src/Nautilus/Interface/HashMap/ChainedHashMap/ChainedHashMap.cpp (sketch)
AbstractHashMapEntry* ChainedHashMap::insertEntry(
    const HashFunction::HashValue::raw_type hash,
    AbstractBufferProvider* bufferProvider)
{
    // Step 0: lazy bucket-array initialisation
    if (entries == nullptr) [[unlikely]] {
        const auto totalSpace = (numberOfChains + 1) * sizeof(ChainedHashMapEntry*);
        entryBuffer = bufferProvider->getUnpooledBuffer(totalSpace);
        entries = reinterpret_cast<ChainedHashMapEntry**>(
            entryBuffer.getAvailableMemoryArea().data());
        std::memset(entries, 0, entryBuffer->getBufferSize());
    }
    // Step 1: allocate a new storage page if the current one is full
    if (numberOfTuples % entriesPerPage == 0) {
        storageSpace.emplace_back(bufferProvider->getUnpooledBuffer(pageSize).value());
    }
    // Step 2: locate the next entry slot in the current page
    const auto pageIndex = numberOfTuples / entriesPerPage;
    auto& bufferStorage = storageSpace[pageIndex];
    const auto entryOffset =
        (numberOfTuples - pageIndex * entriesPerPage) * entrySize;
    // Step 3: chain at bucket head (head of bucket's linked list)
    const auto entryPos = hash & mask;
    auto* const newEntry = new (
        bufferStorage.getAvailableMemoryArea().subspan(entryOffset).data())
        ChainedHashMapEntry(hash);
    newEntry->next = entries[entryPos];
    entries[entryPos] = newEntry;
    ++numberOfTuples;
    return newEntry;
}
```

Four observations.

**The bucket array is allocated lazily.** First insertion
allocates `(numberOfChains + 1) * sizeof(pointer)` bytes via an
unpooled buffer (sized for the array, not the standard 8 KiB).
Empty hash maps cost nothing.

**Entries are stored in a sequence of pages.** Each page is one
`TupleBuffer` from the pool; once full, a new buffer is
allocated. This is what "paged across TupleBuffers" means in
practice — the hash map is not one contiguous arena, it is a
vector of pages, and the buffer pool is the allocator.

**Insertion is at the *head* of the bucket chain.** Newly-
inserted entries are visited first by probes. For a join where
the most recently inserted records are the most likely matches,
this is faster than tail insertion.

**The mask is a power-of-two AND.** `hash & mask` requires
`mask = numberOfChains - 1` and `numberOfChains` to be a
power of two. This is faster than modulo and standard for
in-memory hash tables; the cost is that the chain count must
round up to a power of two.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 16.1: a hash join in flight"}
For `SELECT * FROM r JOIN s ON r.k = s.k INTO matched`, the build
side accumulates `r`'s tuples until `r`'s watermark advances past
the join window's end. Suppose `r` has 100,000 tuples; the hash
map holds 100,000 entries, paged across roughly 30 buffers (each
holding ~3,300 entries depending on entry size).

When `s`'s tuples arrive, the probe operator hashes each, jumps
to the entry, walks the collision chain (typically one or two
entries per bucket if the hash function is good), and emits one
output tuple per match. After the join window closes, the
operator handler tears down the hash map, releasing 30 buffers
back to the pool.
:::

## 16.3 Aggregation state {#sec-aggregation-state}

A windowed aggregation's state is also a hash map, but the values
are *partial aggregates*, not records:

- For `SUM(x)`: value is `(running_sum, count)`.
- For `AVG(x)`: value is `(running_sum, count)`, with the average
  computed at probe time.
- For `MIN(x)`: value is `(running_min)`.
- For `COUNT(*)`: value is `(count)`.

These are small, fixed-size, and combinable. The build side
combines incoming tuples into partial aggregates; the probe side,
when a window fires, walks the hash map and emits one record per
key with the final aggregate value.

For sliding windows where multiple windows can be live
simultaneously, the state grows linearly in the number of active
windows. The engine partitions state by window: each (window,
key) pair gets its own hash-map entry. When a window fires *and*
all sliding windows that include the same data have either fired
or been GC'd, the state for that window is freed.

---

## 16.4 The slice abstraction {#sec-slices}

Window state has a finite lifetime: it lives until the window
fires, plus a grace period for late data, then it can be released.
The engine's mechanism for this is the *slice*.

A slice is a contiguous time range of state. For tumbling windows
of size 1 second, every slice is also 1 second. For sliding
windows of size 5 seconds, advancing every 1 second, the slice
boundary is the GCD of the size and advance — 1 second. The
mechanic is in `WindowSlicesStoreInterface` (in
`nes-physical-operators/include/`).

When a tuple arrives with event-time timestamp `t`, it is assigned
to a slice. Each slice has an end time `t_end`; when the engine's
notion of progress crosses `t_end`, the slice can be probed (its
windows fire) and, after the probe, garbage collected.

The handler is `WindowBasedOperatorHandler`, defined in
`nes-physical-operators/include/`:

```cpp
// nes-physical-operators/include/WindowBasedOperatorHandler.hpp (sketch)
class WindowBasedOperatorHandler : public OperatorHandler {
    std::unique_ptr<WindowSlicesStoreInterface> sliceAndWindowStore;
    std::unique_ptr<MultiOriginWatermarkProcessor> watermarkProcessorBuild;
    std::unique_ptr<MultiOriginWatermarkProcessor> watermarkProcessorProbe;
public:
    WindowBasedOperatorHandler(
        const std::vector<OriginId>& inputOrigins,
        const OriginId outputOriginId,
        std::unique_ptr<WindowSlicesStoreInterface> sliceAndWindowStore);
    void setWorkerThreads(uint64_t numberOfWorkerThreads);
    void checkAndTriggerWindows(const BufferMetaData&, PipelineExecutionContext*);
    virtual void triggerSlices(
        const std::map<WindowInfoAndSequenceNumber,
                       std::vector<std::shared_ptr<Slice>>>&,
        PipelineExecutionContext*) = 0;
};
```

The handler holds **two `MultiOriginWatermarkProcessor`s**:
`watermarkProcessorBuild` for input origins and
`watermarkProcessorProbe` for the single output origin (the
output of the operator becomes a new origin in its own right —
see Chapter 7). The constructor wires them up:

```cpp
// nes-physical-operators/src/WindowBasedOperatorHandler.cpp (sketch)
WindowBasedOperatorHandler::WindowBasedOperatorHandler(
    const std::vector<OriginId>& inputOrigins,
    const OriginId outputOriginId,
    std::unique_ptr<WindowSlicesStoreInterface> sliceAndWindowStore)
    : sliceAndWindowStore(std::move(sliceAndWindowStore)),
      watermarkProcessorBuild(
          std::make_unique<MultiOriginWatermarkProcessor>(inputOrigins)),
      watermarkProcessorProbe(
          std::make_unique<MultiOriginWatermarkProcessor>(
              std::vector{outputOriginId}))
{}
```

`checkAndTriggerWindows` is called as buffers arrive and
watermarks advance. It examines the build watermark, identifies
any slices whose end time has been crossed, and calls
`triggerSlices` for them. `triggerSlices` is operator-specific —
for an aggregation, it walks the per-slice hash maps and emits
one tuple per group.

Each window slice carries a hash map *per worker thread*:

```cpp
// nes-physical-operators/include/Aggregation/AggregationSlice.hpp (sketch)
class AggregationSlice final : public HashMapSlice {
public:
    HashMap* getHashMapPtr(WorkerThreadId workerThreadId) const;
    HashMap* getHashMapPtrOrCreate(WorkerThreadId workerThreadId);
};
```

Per-thread hash maps avoid contention on the hot path: each
worker writes into its own shard. At trigger time, the probe
phase merges shards before emitting results. This is a
classical sharding-vs-locking trade-off, and the code chose
sharding.

A small state-machine governs each window's lifetime:
`WINDOW_FILLING` → `EMITTED_TO_PROBE` (or
`WAITING_ON_TERMINATION` on shutdown). The store advances
windows through these states based on watermark progress; once
emitted, the slice's storage is eligible for garbage collection.

---

## 16.5 Concurrent state, safely {#sec-concurrent-state}

State is shared between worker threads. Multiple workers can
simultaneously be inserting into the same build's hash map, or
probing the same join's state, or accumulating into the same
window's partial aggregates.

NebulaStream handles concurrency in three layers.

**Lock-free at the hash-map level.** The hash map's insertion uses
atomic CAS for slot acquisition. Two workers inserting different
keys do not contend; two workers inserting the same key contend
briefly on the value-chain head pointer.

**Per-window watermark coordination.** Two watermark processors
live on each `WindowBasedOperatorHandler`: one tracks the build
side, one tracks the probe side. The watermarks are advanced
atomically; a window's transition from "open" to "ready to fire"
is a single atomic check.

**Coarse-grained for less-contended state.** State that is not on
the hot path (the slice store metadata, the per-handler GC list)
is protected by a `folly::Synchronized` wrapper, which is
essentially a mutex with a more ergonomic API.

The engine chooses lock-freedom on the hot paths and locks
elsewhere — the standard concurrent-data-structures trade-off.

---

## 16.6 Garbage collection {#sec-gc}

State has to be released. The engine releases it conservatively
via the slice-and-watermark machinery from Chapter 7:

1. A slice is "complete" when all upstream watermarks have passed
   the slice's end time.
2. A complete slice is "fired" — its windows trigger and emit
   results.
3. After firing, the slice is "garbage" — eligible for release.
4. The handler's `garbageCollectSlicesAndWindows` walks the
   garbage list and frees the underlying buffers.

The release is to the buffer pool, not to the OS. Buffers go back
into the pool's queue and are immediately available for reuse by
fresh state.

Late-arriving data that targets a freed slice is *dropped*, not
re-incorporated. This matches the engine's overall stance: when in
doubt, prefer correctness over leniency. Flink's "late side
output" mechanism would be a future addition.

A note worth making before this chapter ends: NebulaStream's
*execution-state* — the hash maps and PagedVectors we have been
discussing — is in-memory only. There is no checkpointing path
yet that would let a worker crash and resume from a snapshot.
What does exist is a small piece of *client-side query
metadata* persistence in `nes-frontend/apps/cli/QueryStateBackend.hpp`
that records query IDs and timestamps under
`~/.local/state/nebucli/`. That is REPL/CLI bookkeeping, not
execution-state recovery. The two are easy to confuse;
Chapter 22 spells out the difference.

---

## Summary {#sec-ch16-summary}

Stateful operators in NebulaStream own their state through
operator handlers, which are runtime objects identified by an
`OperatorHandlerId` and shared between the build and probe halves
of the operator. The state is almost always a `HashMap` keyed on
the operator's grouping/join key, possibly with a `PagedVector`
for collision chains or per-key history. Both data structures are
paged across `TupleBuffer`s from the buffer pool, allowing
release back to the pool when a slice's lifetime ends. Concurrency
is handled by lock-free CAS on the hot path and `folly::Synchronized`
locks elsewhere. State is garbage-collected slice-by-slice as
watermarks advance; late-arriving data targeting freed slices is
silently dropped.

---

## Reading exercises {#sec-ch16-exercises}

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 16.1: measure state size"}
Add a counter that logs `getNumberOfTuples()` on the join's hash
map every second. Run a streaming join with two slow streams.
Plot the growth curve. Where does it level off? At what point
does GC start releasing state?
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 16.2: pool pressure on join state"}
Reduce the buffer pool to 32 buffers (Chapter 4 exercise) and
run a join that needs more state than that. What happens? The
hash map should fail to allocate; the engine should signal
backpressure all the way up to sources. Trace the propagation.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 16.3: late data drop"}
Modify a tumbling-window test to inject a tuple whose event time
is far in the past — older than the most recently fired window.
Confirm that the tuple is dropped silently. What log line
records the drop, if any?
:::
